opener.heading: Week 42: Space Explorers 🚀
about: Azlyn builds a rocket she can sit inside on Friday, and it stands in the hallway until Thursday. Everything after that feeds it: a sealed letter taped above the control panel, a tray of craters she makes herself, ten coins spent on supplies, a mission control desk at the far end of the hall, a shoebox of things you cannot get in space. She is running one long game across seven days and the box in the hallway is what holds it together.

No holiday lands this week, but two threads outlast it. The bulbs she plants on Tuesday come up in March, so the pot by the back door becomes a five-month wait she checks on herself. Then on Thursday afternoon she picks three things out of the week's pile, walks them round to a neighbor and knocks on the door. Leave the rocket standing as long as she wants it, even when it is in the way of the stroller.
azlyn: Changing one thing at a time. Drop height, balloon size, parachute width. She predicts the result, tests it, and puts the two outcomes side by side.
Counting out money that runs out. Ten coins, priced goods, a shelf longer than the purse, and the choice about what goes back.
Reading a sequence of pictures left to right. The recipe card tells her what to do next, and she ticks off where she has got to.
Depth, spacing and waiting. Bulbs set three deep and a fist apart, then five months of nothing happening above the soil.
Speaking to somebody who is not you. Dictating a letter, calling a checklist the length of the hall, saying her own line on a doorstep.
you: A letter teaches her that writing is aimed at someone
Borrowing and returning is her first experience of trusted ownership
Money is a story about exchange long before it's arithmetic
Your own day's work is more interesting to her than you think
Children learn to care about a place by improving it
Reading a recipe is her first experience of print that tells you what to do
Handing something over in person is a separate skill from making it
shopping: A large box, tall enough for Azlyn to sit up inside
A second big box, or a wide box lid, for the mission control desk
Clean jar lids, 4-6, wider than his mouth
Sticky labels, a sheet or two, or paper and tape
A clipboard, or card and a bulldog clip
A craft knife or heavy scissors, for cutting the rocket (adult only)
A flashlight with fresh batteries, and spare batteries
Heavy books, 4–6, to weight the base of the rocket
A cushion for the floor of it
An old sheet or towel you don't mind covered in flour
Plastic grocery bags, 2–3, or a trash bag
A small jar with a screw lid
A kitchen timer, or the clock on the stove
Stones and marbles, 5–6 in different sizes, and a golf ball if you have one
A large mixing bowl and 4 small bowls
A spoon, a wooden spoon and an empty cup
A baking tray and baking paper
An orange, or a ball about that size
Blueberries, for the Big Dipper in a bowl on Friday
10–12 cans and boxes from the cupboard to stock the shop (rice, a washcloth, a can, a blanket, bandages)
Spring bulbs, 20–30, or a garlic bulb to split into cloves
A trowel, or a big metal spoon
A stiff outdoor brush, and a hand brush for Kreston
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 16 months this week. He stacks four blocks, copies whatever chore is in front of him, and has ten words or so. He carries leaves to the pile, posts offcuts through the rocket window, and hands you every stone on the sidewalk.

days.title: The Rocket in the Hallway
days.prepTonight: Stand the big box upright at the end of the hallway. Foil, tape and card go on a shelf she cannot reach.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Message She Sends to Space

opening.title: The Cone on Top
opening.need: the big box · 1 sheet thick card · 1 roll masking tape · 1 roll kitchen foil · 1 permanent marker.
steps: Roll the card into a cone, wide end down. You hold the point, she tapes the seam and then the rest of it however she likes.
Wrap the cone in foil and let her press it down onto the card. The creases stay in.

Stand it on top of the big box you stood at the end of the hallway last night and step back with her. Ask what the box has to become for a nose cone to make sense, and write her answer on the side in marker.

main.title: The Rocket She Fits Inside
materials: 1 large box, tall enough for her to sit up in
1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
2 sheets thick card: this morning's cone, and one for the fins
1 roll masking tape
1 roll kitchen foil
1 permanent marker
4–6 bottle caps or buttons for the panel
4–6 heavy books to weight the base
1 cushion for the floor of it
steps: Run your hand round the inside of the box for staples. Then let her sit in it and mark the door and the window from the inside, in marker.
Cut the door on three sides so it swings, and the window where she marked. She stands back while you cut, and the knife goes back on the shelf between cuts.
Lay the books flat in the bottom around the edges and the cushion on top of them. The base is heavy now and the box takes her weight.
Tape the cone on. Cut two fins from the second sheet of card and tape them low on the outside, on the sides she picks.
She draws the control panel inside the door. You tape the bottle caps on as switches, proud of the card so they move under her thumb.
Get out and leave her in it. Wrap a band of foil round the outside if she wants one. The rocket stands in the hallway until Thursday.
main.tip: Tape the tops on loose enough to rock. She presses them all week.

outside.title: Countdown Into the Leaves
paras: Kick the fallen leaves into one heap in the yard or the park. Mid-October is when the big trees let go, so the pile builds fast. Count down from ten and she jumps in on zero. Build it back up and go again.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies chores. Hand him one fistful of leaves at a time to carry to the pile. By the third go he says the last word of the countdown with you. Keep him to the side of the heap she jumps into.

second.title: The Message She Sends to Space
second.intro: Somebody finds the rocket one day and works out who lived here. Azlyn decides what they get told.
materials: 4 sheets plain paper
1 envelope
Crayons
1 marker
Masking tape
The rocket from this morning, standing in the hallway
Your phone, to photograph every page before it is sealed
steps: Sit on the floor with the paper and ask what a stranger should know about this house. Write it word for word, wrong grammar and all.
Read it back in her own words. She will correct you, and the correction goes in too.
Second sheet: she draws everyone who lives here in crayon, and you write the names underneath as she tells you who is who.
Third sheet is the house from outside. The fourth is hers, for whatever she wants on it.
Photograph all four pages before anything gets folded.
Fold them into the envelope and seal it. She writes on the front in marker, and that is the address.
Tape the envelope inside the rocket, above the panel, where she can see it and not reach it.
second.tip: Kreston will come out bigger than the house and you will have no arms. Leave both.

alternatives: Mail a letter to Grandma and let her drop it in the box.
Draw the house from the inside, one room to a sheet.
Dictate the message into your phone instead.
Tape a paper pocket inside the rocket for her to fill.
outAgain: The café, a window seat and one cake, and she watches who goes past
The park, for the swing and another leaf pile
A friend's house, if anyone can take a visitor at short notice
The corner store, and she pays for the foil you have used half of
Nowhere, if the rocket has her and nobody wants coats on

aroundWorld.title: The Pictures People See in the Sky 🌌
paras: Seven bright stars sit above the house tonight, and the picture drawn round them depends on who is looking. British families call them the Plough, American ones the Big Dipper, and in France the same seven are a saucepan. Aboriginal astronomers in Australia look at a different part of the sky altogether, and they read the dark dust lanes of the Milky Way rather than the stars. The shape they find in the gaps is an emu.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Spoon yogurt into a bowl and drop seven blueberries on top in the Big Dipper's shape, four for the bowl and three for the handle. She eats the handle first.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: The Emu in the Sky is made of the gaps, so you find it by looking at the dark.

days.krestonPM: Give him the offcuts from the door and the window. At 16 months he posts things through gaps. Hold a scrap to the window hole, let him push it through to Azlyn inside, and she hands it back.

insight.headline: A letter teaches her that writing is aimed at someone.
paras: Azlyn has watched you write for two years without seeing where any of it goes. An envelope closes that loop. She dictates, watches her own words turn into marks on a page, and the marks then travel to a person who is not in the room. Children dictating to an adult produce longer and better organized sentences than they can write for years afterwards, because someone else carries the mechanics. Naming the reader before she starts changes what she chooses to say, and sealing the envelope in front of her fixes the idea that writing is a thing you send.

days.safety: The craft knife and heavy scissors are adult-only and go back on the shelf between cuts, not the arm of the sofa. Check inside the box for staples before either child touches it. A tall box tips, and Kreston walks now and will pull on it, so keep the books in the base and keep him out of the rocket while she is climbing in and out. Bottle caps and buttons are the size Kreston chokes on at 16 months, so they stay in your pocket until each one is taped down, and you run a thumb along the row every morning the rocket stands in the hall and press any loose one back down.

days.title: Moon Dust and Craters
days.prepTonight: Put the roasting pan, the flour, the cocoa and the sieve out on an old sheet. Check the batteries in the good flashlight.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Flashlight She Has to Give Back

opening.title: Sifting the Moon Dust
opening.need: 1 old sheet or towel · 1 deep roasting pan · 8 cups all-purpose flour (1 kg) · 2 tbsp cocoa powder · 1 sieve.
steps: Spread the sheet on the kitchen floor and stand the pan in the middle. Everything happens on the sheet today.
She sifts flour through the sieve into the pan until it lies two fingers deep, then smooths the top with the side of her hand.
Sift the cocoa over the top so the whole tray goes gray. Leave it untouched until 9:15 and tell her nothing about what comes next.

main.title: The Craters She Makes Herself
materials: The sifted tray of moon dust, on its sheet
5–6 stones and marbles in different sizes, a golf ball if you have one
1 sieve
1 small pitcher of spare flour and 1 tbsp spare cocoa for the rebuild
1 spoon and 1 empty cup for fishing the stones back out
steps: Kneel her at the edge of the sheet. Drop one marble from a hand's height and look at what it leaves: a hole, a rim, pale flour thrown across the dark cocoa.
Same marble, dropped from as high as she can reach. Put the two holes side by side and ask which one came from higher up. The tray answers for her.
Now change the other thing. Biggest stone and smallest stone, both from the same height she used last time. She will tell you which one mattered more.
Fish every stone and marble out with the spoon, counting them into the cup.
Rebuild: sieve spare flour over the tray, smooth it, dust the cocoa back on. A minute's work and she has a clean moon.
Then let her drop everything she is allowed to drop, in any order, until the tray is holes on holes.
main.tip: Say nothing between drops. The tray keeps every crater, so all four are still in front of her when you get to the rebuild.

outside.title: The Moon Rock Hunt
paras: Take a bag out and collect stones, one rule only: bigger than her fist. Weigh them two at a time in her hands and keep both, saying which is heavier each time. Come home with five and line them up on the step, lightest to heaviest. October drizzle helps: a wet stone shows its color.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and hands things over now. He picks up everything on the sidewalk, so take each one as it comes. Give him one stone too big for his mouth to carry to the bag.

second.title: The Flashlight She Has to Give Back
second.intro: The good flashlight comes off the shelf on terms: it is yours, she can use it, it goes back at the end.
materials: 1 good flashlight with fresh batteries
1 orange, or a ball about that size
1 white plate
1 chair
A dark hallway, or a room with the curtains shut
steps: Hand it over on those terms and let her carry it to the room herself.
Shut the curtains and give her two minutes to sweep the beam round the walls. The novelty burns off fast and then she can hear you.
Stand the chair in the middle, the white plate on it, the orange on the plate so it cannot roll. The plate throws light back up under it.
She holds the flashlight to one side and lights half the orange. Put your finger on the line where the bright side meets the dark.
Keep her flashlight hand still and walk a circle round the chair, saying what you see from each side: all of it lit, half, a sliver, none.
Swap. She walks the circle while you hold the beam steady and calls out how much of the orange is bright from where she stands.
Curtains open, flashlight off, and she puts it back on the shelf herself.
second.tip: She will point it at your face. Turn your head, carry on talking, and it runs out inside a minute.

alternatives: Flashlight and hand shadows on the hallway wall, nothing else.
Cover the flashlight with a candy wrapper and light the orange again.
Take the flashlight into the rocket and shut the door.
outAgain: The lakeshore, for flat stones and the wind off the water
The woods, for a bag of buckeyes
The park, if the drizzle holds off
A drive hunting the moon in daylight, windows down and the heating on
Home, and a second tray of moon dust
days.krestonPM: At the lakeshore he heads for the water, so he stays inside your arm's reach the whole time you are near the edge. He is 16 months and stacks four blocks: pick him five flat stones wider than his own fist, well back from the edge, and let him build. He knocks it down himself and starts again.

insight.headline: Borrowing and returning is her first experience of trusted ownership.
paras: Handing Azlyn the real flashlight, on terms, gives her something a flashlight of her own cannot. She holds a thing that stays yours, uses it under conditions she agreed to, and gives it back working. Three-year-olds sort ownership in stages: mine first, then yours, and last the awkward middle category of borrowed, which carries an obligation stretched across an hour. Saying the whole contract out loud in one sentence lets her hold all three parts of it at once. She puts it back on the shelf and finds out that being trusted with something is a thing she can do.

days.safety: Marbles and small stones are the right size to choke a 16-month-old, and they roll out of the tray. Count them in and out, work on the sheet, and sweep the floor before Kreston goes down anywhere near it. The only stones that go to him are the ones you hand him, every one of them wider than his fist. Loose flour travels, so keep it off the floor he crawls and walks on.

days.title: The Supply Shop
days.prepTonight: Cut ten coins out of thick card and leave them in a paper bag on the table with the sticky labels and a marker.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Purse and the Price Labels

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Ten Coins for the Whole Mission

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Planet Walk Down the Street

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Balloon That Flies Down the String

opening.title: The Purse and the Price Labels
opening.need: 10–12 real things from the cupboards · sticky labels, or paper and tape · 1 marker · 1 tray.
steps: Walk the kitchen with her and let her pick what an astronaut needs. Take her choices at face value, including the can of corn.
Write a price on a label for each, nothing above three, and she sticks them on. Say the number out loud as you write it.
Line the shop up on the tray with the prices facing out. Tell her it opens at 9:15 and she gets ten coins.

main.title: Ten Coins for the Whole Mission
materials: 10 card coins, cut last night from 1 sheet of thick card
1 paper bag or envelope as the purse
The 10–12 labeled supplies from this morning (rice, a washcloth, a can, a blanket, bandages)
Spare sticky labels and 1 marker, for re-pricing
1 tray or box as the shop counter
The rocket in the hallway, from Friday
steps: Set the tray on the table with you behind it. Count the ten coins into the paper bag out loud and hand it to her.
Open the shop. Everything costs what its label says. She counts coins out of the bag into your hand, and you pass the goods across.
She runs out. Hold the silence here and let her work at it, however long that takes.
Then offer the rule that fixes it: anything she brings back, she gets the coins for. She chooses what she can do without.
Second run, and the market changes. Re-label the blanket at five and the bandages at one, then let her look at the shelf again.
Load what she bought into the rocket and count what is left in the bag with her.
main.tip: Do not rescue her at the moment the coins run out.

outside.title: The Planet Walk Down the Street
paras: Put a buckeye down at the front gate for the sun. Walk out counting paces and lay something at each planet: a stone for Mercury three paces on, a leaf for Earth at ten, an acorn for Jupiter fifty paces further than she expects. She gives up around Saturn. Pick it all back up on the way home.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and walks the whole street now. Let him out of the stroller for the middle stretch and give him the leaf to carry, because the stones and the acorns stay in your hand. He passes it to Azlyn to put down.

second.title: The Balloon That Flies Down the String
second.intro: A balloon lets its air out of the back and shoves itself forward. On a string, it goes where the string goes.
materials: 6–8 balloons
2–3 drinking straws, or a cardboard tube cut into short rings
1 ball of string, 13 feet
Masking tape
2 dining chairs, or a door handle and a chair
1 clothespin or small toy as cargo
steps: Thread the string through a straw, tie it between the two chair backs and pull it tight, one end higher than the other.
Blow a balloon up and pinch the neck shut. Do not tie it.
Tape the balloon under the straw, neck pointing back at the high end. Two strips, one each side.
She counts down from five and lets go. Every launch is hers to release.
Change one thing at a time and run it again: fuller balloon, slacker string, both ends level. She calls it before each go.
Tape the clothespin on as cargo and see whether it still makes the far end.
Take the string down the second you finish, count the balloons back and pocket the lot.
second.tip: She cannot blow these up and she will be furious about it. Give her the neck to pinch while you tape.

alternatives: Let balloons go across the room untethered and chase them.
Run the shop again with her behind the counter.
Tape a straw to a paper cup and blow it along the table.
outAgain: The sunset walk, pushed to four so the light goes as you turn for home
The playground, and count what you spend on nothing
The duck pond, with a bag of oats or defrosted peas and never bread
The corner store, and she pays with real coins this time
days.krestonPM: Keep him out of the room while the balloons are up. Afterwards, give him the empty paper purse and a handful of jar lids too wide for his mouth. At 16 months he posts them in and tips them out again for five or ten minutes, then comes back to it twice more before dinner.

insight.headline: Money is a story about exchange long before it's arithmetic.
paras: Azlyn cannot do the sum yet, but she can do the trade. She holds the whole idea that the coins go one way, the can comes the other way, and the coins are then gone. That last part is what shop play teaches and a piggy bank does not. Counting three coins into your hand also does more for her number sense than counting three of anything on a page, because each coin buys something and the total decides what she gets. Give her a fixed ten and let the shelf outlast them, and she meets scarcity in a form small enough to survive.

days.safety: A burst balloon is the worst choking hazard in the house for a child Kreston's age. Count the balloons, pick up every scrap the second one goes, and keep the pieces in your pocket rather than a trash can he can reach. Take the string down and put it away the moment you finish, because a line at toddler height is a strangulation risk. The card coins are mouth-size discs, so they stay up on the table with Azlyn and Kreston posts the jar lids, which are too wide for his mouth. Count all ten coins back into the bag at the end. Keep Kreston on your hand for every stretch of the planet walk he is out of the stroller, walk Azlyn on the house side, and stop at every driveway to look.

days.title: Mission Control
days.prepTonight: Cut two strips of card for the headsets, flatten a big box lid for the desk, and buy spring bulbs and a bag of potting soil for tomorrow.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Desk with a Hundred Buttons

opening.title: Two Cups and a Headband
opening.need: 2 card strips · 4 paper cups · 1 roll masking tape.
steps: Tape one strip into a ring that sits on her head without falling over her eyes. Do the second to fit yours.
Tape a paper cup to each side of both bands, open end out. They do nothing, and she will not care.
Put yours on, go into the next room and say her name in a flat radio voice. Wait for her to answer before anything else.

main.title: The Desk with a Hundred Buttons
materials: 1 large box lid, or the flattened front of a box
10–15 bottle caps or buttons
2 wide jar lids and 1 spare strip of card, for Kreston's end
1 roll masking tape
2 markers, one of them red
The two headsets from this morning
1 sheet of paper for the checklist
1 flashlight as the warning light
steps: Lay the lid flat in front of her and leave it blank. She draws the dials, the screens, the numbers and one big red button in the red marker. You draw nothing on it.
Tape the bottle caps on around her drawings, all ten or fifteen, so the desk has switches that move.
Write the checklist on the paper with a small picture beside each line: door, cone, fuel, belt, go. The pictures are what she reads.
Stand the desk at the far end of the hall from the rocket. Headsets on, one of you at each end, and you have to shout the whole length of the hall to be heard.
Read the checklist one line at a time. She presses a switch for each and says done. The flashlight is the warning light: switch it on and she has to find the switch that puts it out.
Swap ends and run it again, so she gets the desk and the seat.
main.tip: Give her the last line of the countdown. A three-year-old who says go stays in a game twice as long.

outside.title: The People Already at Work
paras: Monday morning, and half the street is at work before you leave the house. Count the jobs going on: the garbage truck and the arm that lifts, a van double-parked with the back open, somebody up a ladder, the store pulling its shutters up. Ask what each job is for. Mid-October gives you everybody's breath in the air.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, so a garbage truck is a whole movie to him. Stop the stroller and let him watch the arm go up and come down twice. He waves at the crew and they wave back.

second.title: Clocking On and Clocking Off
second.intro: Azlyn works a real shift this afternoon: a start, a job list, a break, an end, and a look at where Joseph is while she does it.
materials: 1 clipboard, or a piece of card and a bulldog clip
4–5 sheets of paper
1 marker
1 kitchen timer, or the clock on the stove
The mission control desk from this morning, at the far end of the hall
A photo of Joseph's workplace on your phone
steps: Clip a sheet on the board. Write START at the top and the time next to it, and she says when the shift begins.
Draw five jobs down the page as small pictures: check the door, check the cone, count the supplies, fill in the log, press the red button. She ticks each one with the marker as she finishes it.
Set the timer for twenty minutes and leave her at the desk to work.
When it goes, that is her break. Sit down with a drink and show her the photo of where Joseph is standing right now, and what he is doing at this hour.
Second shift, and she picks two new jobs for the list herself, in her own marks, which you leave alone.
Clocking off: she writes the end mark, unclips the sheet and hands it to you.
She takes the log to the front door and props it where Joseph will see it the second he comes in.
second.tip: Do not skip the break. Sitting down because a timer said so is the part of a working day she has never seen.

alternatives: One job on the list, one tick, and out to the park.
Ring Joseph from the desk and read him the checklist.
Draw his workplace from what she remembers of it.
Run the shift with a teddy on the desk and her supervising.
outAgain: The neighborhood park, and clock her back on when you get home
The riverside path, for the leaves coming down on the water
The green space with a ball, after an hour of sitting at a desk
A walk past wherever Joseph works, if it is close enough
Indoor playground, if the rain has set in
days.krestonPM: Tape the two jar lids onto the spare strip of card and give him that at his own end of the room, well away from the desk. At 16 months he copies what he sees, so he presses whichever switch she pressed last. Give him one end of the log to carry to the door with her.

insight.headline: Your own day's work is more interesting to her than you think.
paras: Joseph leaves and comes back and the middle is a blank to Azlyn. She fills it with whatever she has: a room, a chair, a vague sense of far away. Showing her one photo and naming what he is doing at that hour turns the blank into something she can picture and ask about, and children who can picture the work ask better questions about it for months. The shift structure does the rest. Starting, ticking things off, stopping for a break and finishing on purpose gives her the shape of a working day in ninety minutes, from the inside.

days.safety: Buttons and bottle caps are a choking size for a 16-month-old, so the desk itself stays at Azlyn's end and the only switches Kreston gets are the two jar lids, which are too wide for his mouth. Count the caps out at 9:15 and back onto a high shelf at the end, and run a hand over the floor he walks on. The markers go back on the shelf between shifts, out of his reach.

days.title: Bulbs and the Blue Planet
days.prepTonight: Stand the bulbs, the trowel, the potting soil and the pots by the back door. Swimming bag in the car.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Bulbs That Wait Under the Ground

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Leaves Off Next Door's Path

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Box of Things You Can't Get in Space

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Drawing What Went in the Box

opening.title: Counting Out the Bulbs
opening.need: 20–30 spring bulbs · 1 tray · 2 craft sticks · 1 marker.
steps: Tip the bulbs onto the tray and let her turn them over. Show her the pointed end and the hairy flat end, and which way up they go in.
Count them into piles of five, out loud, and let her lose count and start again.
She draws a flower on each craft stick and you write the date beside it. Then both of you wash your hands.

main.title: The Bulbs That Wait Under the Ground
materials: 20–30 spring bulbs from the supermarket. No bulbs: split a garlic bulb into cloves and plant them the same way, which is no less real
1 trowel, or a big metal spoon
2 large pots, or a cleared patch of ground
1 bag of potting soil, or the soil that is already there
1 watering can or pitcher
The 2 labeled craft sticks from this morning
steps: She fills each pot two thirds full with the trowel while you hold it steady. By the second pot she gets more in than out.
Show her the depth: a hole three bulbs deep. Stack three in your hand so she sees the measurement rather than hears a number.
She digs, sets each bulb pointed end up and covers it. A fist apart, measured with her own fist put down between them.
Press the top flat with both palms. Water until it runs out the bottom.
Push the labels in at the front and tell her the month they come up: five months of nothing happening.
Stand the pots where she walks past them every day, and walk her past again this evening.
main.tip: She will want to dig one up next week to check. One pot is hers to dig, the other stays shut, and you hold that line all the way to March.

outside.title: The Leaves Off Next Door's Path
paras: Take a stiff brush and do next door's front path as well as your own, having asked first. Sweep the leaves off the step into a heap at the top of the driveway, well back from the road, and let her do the last stretch on her own. Come past it after swimming and look at what the two of you changed.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, so he wants the brush more than anything else outdoors. Give him a hand brush of his own and let him push leaves wherever he likes. He follows Azlyn down the path doing his version of her job.

second.title: The Box of Things You Can't Get in Space
second.intro: A shoebox holds everything Azlyn would miss if she left. She fills it and you write her reason on each thing.
materials: 1 shoebox with a lid
1 small jar with a screw lid
Paper and 1 marker for the labels
Masking tape
Whatever she picks up outside
Your phone, for the photo of the finished box
steps: Ask what she would miss most and write the list as she says it, in her order, with no steering.
Five minutes out at the door with the box: a leaf, a stone, a handful of grass with soil on it.
Fill the jar from the tap, screw the lid tight, tape round it. Water out of a wall is the strangest thing in there and she has never once thought about it.
One thing from her own room goes in, her choice, and it stays in until Sunday.
Label each thing with what she said about it. Read them back and let her change any.
Lid on, tape round the outside, and she says what goes on the top.
Photograph the box open with everything laid out, because the grass has about a week in it.
second.tip: Ask what she would take for Kreston. She picks something for him without being asked twice.

alternatives: One jar of water and nothing else in it.
Plant the leftover bulbs in a third pot for a neighbor.
Fill the box from indoors only, no coats needed.
outAgain: Swimming, and she wears herself out before the bath
The pool's quiet session, if the after-school crowd is in
Indoor playground, if the pool is closed
Straight home, if swimming has finished them off
days.krestonPM: He comes to swimming and stays within arm's reach in the water, every second. At 16 months he walks the poolside and heads for the edge given a moment. In the water he copies, so blow bubbles where he can see your face and wait for his version.

insight.headline: Children learn to care about a place by improving it.
paras: Azlyn sweeping a neighbor's path leaves her with something no conversation about kindness reaches. She looked at one specific step, changed it, and can see the change on the way past this evening. Three-year-olds attach to places through their own hands, which is why the pot she planted counts for more than the bed you planted, and why she will keep checking her bulbs for five months. Effort is what makes a place hers, and it works on somebody else's doorstep as well as her own. Do the work beside her and stay off the moral. The swept path and the buried bulbs carry it.

days.safety: Daffodil and tulip bulbs are poisonous if eaten and they look like small onions. Count them out, count them in, and keep the bag off the floor while Kreston is loose, because at 16 months everything still goes in his mouth. Both children get their hands washed after soil, before food. Sweeping a front path ends at a road, so the heap stops at the top of the driveway, Kreston brushes on the house side of you, and neither child steps off the curb. At the pool both children stay inside your arm's reach in the water the whole time, and armbands, rings and floats are toys, never safety equipment.

days.title: Space Food
days.prepTonight: Draw the picture recipe on card, one step to a box, left to right. Butter and syrup out on the side.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Eating With Nothing on the Table

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Taping Her Own Toys to the Tray

opening.title: One Bowl for Every Picture
opening.need: the picture recipe card · 4 small bowls · 2 cups rolled oats (200 g) · 2 tbsp cocoa · 3 tbsp honey or corn syrup · 2 tbsp shredded coconut.
steps: Sit her in front of the picture recipe you drew last night and go along the pictures with your finger, left to right. Read the pictures, leave the words.
One bowl under each picture. She tips the oats in and levels the cocoa, you do the syrup, and the coconut goes in last.
Line the four bowls up in the order the pictures give. Ask which comes first and let her move them if she disagrees.

main.title: Moon Rocks You Can Eat
materials: The four measured bowls: 2 cups rolled oats (200 g), 2 tbsp cocoa powder, 3 tbsp honey or corn syrup, 2 tbsp shredded coconut
5 tbsp butter (75 g)
1 large bowl, 1 small saucepan, 1 wooden spoon
1 baking tray and baking paper
The picture recipe card and 1 marker for ticking off
steps: Butter and honey into the pan on the back burner, low heat, you at the stovetop and her the far side of the table. Off the heat the moment the butter has gone.
Oats and cocoa into the large bowl. She stirs them together, then ticks that picture on the card.
Pour the hot mix in yourself and stir it through. Hand her the spoon once the bowl is cool enough to hold with both hands.
Line the tray. Wet hands, and she rolls lumpy rocks. Lumpy is the target, so leave the ugly ones as they come.
Roll a few through the coconut for moon dust, and she ticks the last picture.
Into the fridge for an hour. They belong to the afternoon, so say that now.
main.tip: Let the first three fall apart. She finds the right squeeze by feel.

outside.title: The Buckeye and the Leaf
paras: Find a low wall, one buckeye and one wide leaf. She holds one in each hand, arms out level, and drops both at once. The buckeye wins every time. Air slows the leaf. There is no air on the moon, so an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather there and they landed together. Collect a bagful of buckeyes on the way home.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months. Buckeyes are a choking size, so they stay in the bag with you and he gets leaves. Give him one to drop off the wall and hold his other hand. He drops, watches and wants it back.

second.title: Eating With Nothing on the Table
second.intro: Afternoon snack, the way it works with no gravity. Everything gets taped down.
materials: 4–6 freezer bags
2–3 straws
1 squeezy sauce bottle
Masking tape
1 tray
The moon rocks from this morning
Yogurt, apple pieces and a drink in a cup
steps: Clear the table down to bare wood. Nothing stays on it that is not stuck to it.
Tape the tray to the table by all four corners and push it. It does not move, and that is the rule for the rest.
Yogurt into the squeezy bottle, apple pieces into one bag, moon rocks into another. She loads them.
Tape each bag to the tray by one corner, and the straw and the cup as well.
She eats the apple out of the bag with no hands on the bag, and the yogurt straight out of the bottle. No plates, no bowls, no silverware.
Halfway through, let go of everything at once and see what stays put. The tape is the reason any of it works.
Untape, wipe down, and ask whether she would want dinner like that every night. She will say no.
second.tip: Give her the squeezy bottle for the drink as well as the yogurt.

alternatives: Tape one bag to the tray and stop there.
Eat the whole snack standing up with hands behind her back.
Pack a moon rock into a bag for tomorrow's parachute delivery.
Draw the picture recipe again, her version, for the fridge door.
outAgain: Indoor playground, and it is dark by the time you come out
The library, if this is the week for it
The park, for twenty minutes before the light goes
A drive to look at the first houses with their lights on
Home, and Friday's leaf pile if the wind has left it
days.krestonPM: He gets the same snack, untaped and on a plate. At 16 months he copies everything Azlyn does at a table. Give him a small pot with a lid to pull off and press back on, which is the job he wants at a table anyway.

insight.headline: Reading a recipe is her first experience of print that tells you what to do.
paras: Most print in Azlyn's life describes things: a story, a label, a sign. A recipe on the wall gives instructions, and the instructions have to be followed in order or the thing does not work. Following a picture sequence left to right builds the habit reading needs long before letters do, and she gets the payoff on a tray an hour later. Ticking each picture as she finishes it adds the other half, tracking where she is in a sequence she cannot hold in her head. Leave the card up on the fridge and she will run it again on her own.

days.safety: Melted butter and honey leave the stovetop at scalding heat, so the pan goes to the back burner and she stirs the bowl, never the pan. Keep Kreston out of the kitchen while it is hot. Whole lumps are a choking size for him, so his portion gets pressed flat and broken small. If you swap in nut butter, check it against every allergy in the house first. The freezer bags stay taped to the tray or in your pocket, because a bag over his face is a suffocation risk and it takes seconds.

days.title: Coming Home
days.prepTonight: Put the grocery bags, the string and the clothespins on the top shelf, and message whoever she is walking round to tomorrow so somebody is in.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The First Star Out the Window

opening.title: Packing the Capsule
opening.need: 1 clean yogurt pot · 3–4 clothespins · 1 marker · masking tape.
steps: She draws a face on each peg. Let her name them and write the names on the backs.
One peg goes in the pot as the crew, taped down so it cannot fall out when the pot turns over.
Stand the capsule at the bottom of the stairs with the rest of the crew beside it, waiting for a lift.

main.title: The Slow Way Down
materials: 2–3 plastic grocery bags, or 1 trash bag
1 ball of string
Masking tape
1 pair of adult scissors (adult only)
The 3–4 peg astronauts from this morning
The yogurt pot capsule, peg taped inside
A stairwell, or a chair on a landing
steps: Cut a square out of a grocery bag, about the size of a dish towel, and four short lines of string a hand's length each. You cut, she flattens the square on the floor. The scissors go back on the shelf. Tape one string to each corner.
Tape all four free ends to the rim of the pot. Make a second while you are set up, because one of these gets given away this afternoon.
Top of the stairs, her hand on the rail, both of you back from the edge. She holds it out and lets go, and you both count: one elephant, two elephant.
Change one thing per drop. A bigger square. A hole torn in the middle. Two more pegs in the pot. Count each one.
Drop the pot with no parachute at all so she has something to compare against.
Line the drops up in her words at the end: which one took longest, and what was different about it.
main.tip: The hole in the middle looks like a mistake and it works better. Drop both together, one from each hand.

outside.title: The Wind Takes It Sideways
paras: Take the spare parachute to the top of the slide or a low wall. Late October wind takes it ten feet from where she let go, somewhere different every time. Get her to point at where it will come down before each drop. Chase it, and come home when her hands are too cold.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months. The peg astronauts are choke-sized and the plastic square is a suffocation risk, so both stay with you. Give him a clean empty yogurt pot of his own to carry in one fist while he toddles after Azlyn. Every bag and offcut stays in your pocket.

second.title: Knocking on the Door Herself
second.intro: Azlyn picks something out of the week's pile and walks it round to somebody herself.
materials: Her moon rock, a drawing, and the spare parachute
1 paper bag
Paper and 1 marker for the label
Masking tape
Shoes and a coat
steps: Lay the week's things on the table and let her choose three to give away. Take her choices as they come, including the one you wanted to keep.
She draws a picture for whoever is getting them, and that goes in the bag on top.
She says who the bag is for. Write the name big on the paper, she tapes the label to the front.
Practice once on the kitchen door. Knock, wait, and say the line she picks. Once through and then stop, because a rehearsed child freezes harder.
Coats and shoes, and she carries the bag the whole way, including the stretch where it drags on the sidewalk.
She knocks. Stand one step back and let the pause happen, however long it runs.
Walk home in the dusk and let her tell you what they said, which will not be what they said.
second.tip: Do not fill the silence on the doorstep. Whatever comes out of her is hers.

alternatives: Mail the drawing through the mail slot instead of knocking.
Leave the bag on the step and wave from the gate.
Give it to Joseph at the door when he gets in.
Parachute the bag off the stairs to whoever is at the bottom.
outAgain: The hardware store, for string and a bag of bulbs for the third pot
The market, and she carries one thing home in her own bag
The park, for the slide and one more parachute drop
The corner store, and she hands the money over herself
The walk round to the neighbor, if the delivery slipped to now
days.krestonPM: Bring him on the walk round and let him hold one handle of the paper bag while Azlyn holds the other. At 16 months he has ten words or so, and one of them will come out on the doorstep. Keep him off the road side of the sidewalk.

insight.headline: Handing something over in person is a separate skill from making it.
paras: Azlyn spent twenty minutes on the parachute with no trouble at all. Standing on a step while somebody looks at her is a different task, and she may freeze on it. Handing an object to a near-stranger asks her to hold a plan in her head, read a face, and speak while being watched, all at once, and three-year-olds run out of room. Rehearsing the knock once at the kitchen door gives her a script to fall back on. Letting the silence sit, rather than saying her line for her, is what makes the second delivery easier than the first.

days.safety: A plastic grocery bag over a 16-month-old's face is a suffocation risk and it takes seconds, so every bag and offcut stays with you and goes away the moment you finish. Cut the string lines short. Clothespin astronauts are choking size at 16 months, so none of them go to him and they get counted back into your pocket at the end. She drops from the top step with a hand on the rail, and nothing goes over while Kreston is on the floor below. The scissors stay with you.
